explanation: Heterogeneous. Fires on the second '%' in parallel statistics ('57.2% for stage IB'), on 'risk' after 'increased'/'mortality', on 'worldwide' after disease phrases, and on assorted content nouns that finish a noun phrase (skills, resources, tournaments, client). No single token or context ties these together.

Mixture. The most frequent case is the generic second-person 'you' ('Depends who you ask', 'Generally you don't want'). It also fires on unrelated tokens: a Turkish 'İN', a Spanish 'tu' fragment, name parts ('-K', 'belt'), code tokens and prepositions.

Mixture of formatting tokens. It fires on the 'b'/'B' right after '[@' in citations, on the final '.' of an '. . .' ellipsis, on code tokens (include headers, '.on', '(c)', import paths), on '¿', and on 'that' in 'similar to that seen'.

Degree adverbs and intensifiers that modify an adjective, adverb or quantity: 'pretty', 'very', 'too', 'fairly', 'extremely', Romanian 'mai'. 'pretty' and 'too' fire strongest. 'more'/'quite'/'rather' fire only moderately to weakly.

Mainly perfect-tense 'has'/'have' right after a subject noun or pronoun in scientific prose ('FFA exposure has been shown', 'It has recently been reported'). It also fires on 'a' in sports-result phrases ('take a 25-', 'in a Sunday night maul') and on 'most'/'very' before an adjective.

First subword piece of a rare or multi-token word, mostly medical/anatomical terms ('pal'-mar, 'peric'+'ard'-ial, 'rot'-endinous) and foreign place or proper names ('Lud'-wigsfelde, 'Univers'-ità, 'Bad'-ghis, 'Cont'-roversy/ends). Common whole words do not fire.

Mixed. It fires on 'of' in 'is a species/genus of' taxonomy openers and in 'model of', and on words in medical or descriptive phrases (dil'ated', 'right' side, 'some', 'distinctive', 'soft', 'expanded'). The common thread may be descriptive or encyclopedic prose, but the triggers are inconsistent.

Word-initial subword fragments that begin a longer word split into several tokens, especially 'contr' (contractions, Contrary, contraindications), 'nu', 'sur', 'ser', 'w', 'lymph', 'sar'. Fires on the opening fragment when the rest of the word follows as further tokens, not on whole words.

Mixture. It fires on 'along' and 'of' in GPL license boilerplate, on word-final suffix pieces ('-ing', '-ic', '-ase', '-ings', '-ients'), on commas in dates and name lists, and on math tokens. No coherent trigger.

Mostly the word 'WordPress' (' WordPress', 'wordpress', 'Word Press', 'wp', 'Wordpress' inside identifiers) in web-development contexts. It also fires on the letter after an initial 'W' in acronyms or codes ('WO' patent numbers, 'w3.org', 'WO3', 'W1T').

Mixture. It fires on verbs or prepositions after a subject or modal ('can make it', 'not taking', 'stay focused', 'were enrolled', 'at rest'), on 'after' in news sentences, on 'LICENSE' in BSD headers, and on code tokens ('await', '">'). No clear common feature.

A punctuation or symbol token that directly prefixes a following word with no space, as in a filename extension, framework name, CSS selector, flag or path: '.NET', '.data()', '.php', '#3', '/r/', '-webkit', ':visited', '*only*', '%>%'. Ordinary sentence punctuation fires weakly or not at all.

Mixture. It fires on code tokens (return, '(string', '.com' in URLs, 'while'), on 'least' in 'at least', on 'than' in 'less than', on LaTeX operators, and on 'given'/'for'/'each' in explanatory prose. Little shared structure.

Points where a list or clause continues: the coordinating 'and', 'well' in 'as well as', and commas that join noun phrases or clauses. Weaker on sentence-ending punctuation ('.', '?', '!!!', '. .') and on code delimiters.

The token right after existential or exhaustive constructions: 'There is [no/nothing/every/evidence/ample/a need]', 'we find nothing', 'do everything we (can)', and auxiliaries in 'should be able to', 'may be free to'. Strongest on the quantifier or noun that completes 'there is ...' or 'do everything ...'.

Mixture of identifier fragments. It fires strongest on digits inside U.S. patent numbers ('5,3[8]1'), and also on command-line flags (-exec, -I, 'test', '[['), HTTP header pieces, and chemical-name prefixes ('m[ethyl]', 'hydro[x]').

Mixed and largely unpredictable. It fires on 'sign' in 'dollar sign', on code identifiers ('Value', 'mimeType', '.md'), math variables, 'written' in 'prior written permission', date commas, product names (Firefox) and assorted nouns.

Mostly words for spatial position or periphery: 'side' (side-effects, side project), 'surround', 'around', 'above' (the 'register link above' boilerplate), 'near', and 'site' after 'external' or 'new'. It also fires on the C/Rust keyword 'extern'.

Structural tokens that open a nested block in code or markup, usually an opener followed by a newline: '>⏎' after an XML parent tag, '{⏎', '(⏎', '[⏎', 'key:' before a list or object. Weaker on other code punctuation and almost nothing in prose.

Mixture. It fires on 'as'/'to' after a verb of manner or purpose ('cast as', 'focused as', 'influence to perform'), on paired-group nouns ('men', 'women', 'South Sudan'), and on assorted nouns in descriptive technical or travel prose. No consistent trigger.

Digits that end a citation reference ID in scientific markup: the final number in '[@pone...ref00[1]]', '[@CR[4]]', '[@B[3]]', '[@b1[3]]'. Low digits (1-4) in the first citation of a sentence fire strongest. The surrounding brackets, '@' and '--' fire only moderately.
